title: Explain each SOLID principle with violations and fixes, how SRP and DIP can clash during refactoring, and whether SOLID can lead to over-engineering.
shortTitle: Each SOLID principle with violations and fixes, the SRP–DIP clash, and SOLID over-engineering
keyPoints: SRP violation: a class that validates, transfers, emails, and logs changes for four reasons – split into focused services.
OCP violation: a growing if-else chain on account type – replace with an InterestStrategy interface and one class per type.
LSP violation: a SavingsAccount subclass that throws on withdraw breaks callers written for Account – redesign the hierarchy.
ISP violation: a fat BankingOperations interface forces a savings account to stub out stock trading – split into role interfaces.
DIP violation: a LoanService that does new CibilHttpClient() is welded to one vendor – depend on a CreditScoreProvider interface.
SRP and DIP can clash: aggressive splitting creates many tiny classes needing interfaces between every pair, so only abstract where you expect variation.
SOLID can over-engineer: an interface for a class with one implementation adds indirection for no benefit – apply principles when real pressure appears.

s1_definition.oneliner: SOLID is five rules: one job per class, extend without modifying, subtypes must substitute, small focused interfaces, and depend on abstractions not concretions.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **SOLID** is a set of five object-oriented design principles that produce code easier to maintain, extend, and test.
- **S – Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)** – a class should have only one reason to change.
- **O – Open/Closed Principle (OCP)** – software should be open for extension but closed for modification.
- **L – Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)** – objects of a subtype must be usable anywhere the supertype is expected without breaking correctness.
- **I – Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)** – no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use.
- **D – Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)** – high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not low-level concrete classes.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of running National Bank of India cleanly. Single Responsibility means each employee has one clear job: the cashier only handles cash, the auditor only audits. Open/Closed means when you add a new loan product you open a new counter rather than rebuilding the whole branch. Liskov means any teller assigned to a counter must be able to do that counter's job properly. Interface Segregation means you do not force the cashier to also know the fire-safety manual. Dependency Inversion means the loan manager depends on the idea of a credit-check service, not on one specific vendor.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  SOLID Principles – What Each One Attacks
  ─────────────────────────────────────────

  SRP ─── Too many reasons to change in one class
           │
           ▼
  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │TransferService│   │NotificationSvc│   │StatementSvc  │
  │(transfer only)│   │(email only)   │   │(PDF only)    │
  └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘

  OCP ─── Adding behaviour requires editing existing code
           │
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ InterestStrategy  │ ◄── interface
  └──────┬───────────┘
         ├──── SavingsInterest
         ├──── CurrentInterest
         └──── NreInterest  (new class, no edits)

  LSP ─── Subtype breaks parent's contract
           │
           ▼
  Caller expects: account.withdraw(amount) works
  Violation: FixedDepositAccount.withdraw() throws!

  ISP ─── Fat interface forces unused implementations
           │
           ▼
  Split: DepositOps + TradingOps + CardOps

  DIP ─── High-level depends on low-level concrete class
           │
           ▼
  ┌────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ LoanService │────▶│ CreditScoreProvider │ ◄── interface
  └────────────┘     └──────────┬──────────┘
                                ├── CibilProvider
                                └── ExperianProvider
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
SOLID is five object-oriented design principles that together make code easier to maintain, extend, and test. Single Responsibility says a class should have only one reason to change, so Rajesh splits a class that did transfers, emails, and PDF generation into three focused services at National Bank of India. Open/Closed says code should be open for extension but closed for modification, which he achieves by replacing a growing if-else chain with a strategy interface per account type, so adding a product is a new class, not an edit.

Liskov Substitution says a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking the contract, so a `FixedDepositAccount` must not throw from `withdraw` if callers rely on `Account.withdraw` working. Interface Segregation says do not force a class to implement methods it does not need, so Pankaj keeps interfaces small and focused. Dependency Inversion says high-level policy should depend on abstractions, not concrete low-level classes, so services depend on interfaces and receive implementations by injection.

The interesting tension the interviewer usually probes is how SRP and DIP can clash during refactoring. When Rajesh aggressively splits classes to honour SRP, the pieces must collaborate, and if he puts an interface between every pair to honour DIP, the result is an explosion of tiny one-method classes and pointless single-implementation interfaces that are harder to read than the original. The resolution is to split only along genuine, independent reasons to change, and introduce an abstraction only where variation is expected or a testing seam is needed.

That leads to the honest answer on over-engineering: SOLID can absolutely cause over-engineering if applied dogmatically. An interface for a class that will only ever have one implementation adds indirection for no benefit. Pankaj treats SOLID as tools to manage change and coupling where they genuinely exist: start simple and cohesive, and apply a principle when a real pressure appears.

Remember one sentence: SOLID is five principles that manage change and coupling, but applied dogmatically they over-engineer, so split by real reasons to change and abstract only where you expect variation.
